idiom_name: std::sync::Mutex/RwLock strategy (or a generic policy parameter) with the guard as the scoped lock
implementation_notes: std::sync::Mutex and RwLock are the policy family and their guards are Scoped Locking by construction: lock() or read()/write() returns a MutexGuard/RwLockReadGuard whose Drop releases the lock, so the guard class is unnecessary and forgetting to release requires std::mem::forget. Because Mutex<T> owns the data it protects, the type system makes it impossible to touch the state without going through the policy - a stronger guarantee than the classic pattern, where a missing guard is a silent defect. The policy is selected at the composition root by the field's type or by a generic parameter/trait bound, and parking_lot::Mutex/RwLock is a drop-in alternative that the crate describes as smaller, faster and more flexible than the standard library types; std's poisoning (is_poisoned/clear_poison) turns a panic inside a critical section into an error that every later locker must handle, which is the main reason to prefer one or the other.
pitfalls: Poisoning makes every panic inside a critical section an error for all later lockers; decide deliberately (recover with clear_poison, propagate, or choose parking_lot) instead of unwrapping blindly.
Lock ordering across two policies deadlocks regardless of which types implement them, and RwLock cannot upgrade: taking a read lock and then a write lock in the same thread is a documented deadlock.

Send/Sync bounds are part of the policy choice - a non-Sync strategy (Rc<RefCell<..>>) only compiles for single-threaded components, so a strategized component must be generic over the bound or the strategy wrapped in Arc.
